title: A protective chant
hookLine: a verse of protection given by the spirit kings

cards: It's late at night on Vulture's Peak, above Rajagaha, and the hill lights up. The Four Great Kings have come, the guardians of the four directions in Buddhist cosmology, each with a vast retinue of spirits.

Vessavana, guardian of the north, speaks for them. Some spirits trust the Buddha's teaching, he says, and some don't. And your monks and nuns live alone, in forests and empty places, where those spirits roam.
So we've brought something: a verse they can say, to stay safe and at ease.

teach.b: This is the Atanatiya Sutta, the thirty-second Long Discourse, named, tradition says, for Atanata, the city where the verses were composed. Vessavana recites the protection, and the Buddha consents by silence.

In the morning he tells the monks what happened, repeats the verses, and says: learn this protection, master it, remember it. It's for your benefit, for the safety and ease of monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen.
It begins with homage to seven Buddhas, starting with Vipassi, the prince of the four sights from a few weeks back, and ending with Gotama.
Then it honors each of the four directions and its guardian king, where the sun rises and where it sets. It names the awakened first, then faces outward, all the way round.
The Pali word for these verses is paritta, a protection, a safeguard. And this is one of the roots of a practice you can still hear today.
In Theravada countries, monks chant parittas to bless a new house, beside the sick, and in times of danger, sometimes holding a white thread that links everyone present.
People understand the protection in different ways: as real help from beings who honor the Buddha, as the power of the truth spoken, or as the calm that comes over a mind reminded of what it trusts.
The sutta itself simply gives the verses, and asks that they be learned.

how: In Theravada countries monks chant paritta verses at blessings, illnesses and new beginnings, often holding a white cord that links everyone present, and the Atanatiya verses are part of the larger paritta collection.

games.q: you're the Buddha. at night the Four Great Kings offer a protective verse for monks living alone in the forest. what do you do?
o: refuse it: monks need no protection.
consent by silence, then teach it to the monks the next morning.
keep it secret for advanced students.
games.why: he consents silently, and in the morning tells the monks to learn and remember it for their safety and ease.

practice: If you chant, say slowly, three times as it's traditionally said, the homage that opens Theravada chanting: namo tassa bhagavato arahato samma-sambuddhassa, homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, fully awakened.
If you'd rather not chant, turn your attention one at a time to the four directions around you, front, right, behind, left, and feel steady at the center.

wordCard.voice: paritta. The Atanatiya verses, given by the Four Great Kings in DN 32, honoring seven Buddhas and the four directions. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali paritta: protection, safeguard. the name for protective chants like the Atanatiya verses.

carryVoice: Your line: protection. One line you trust can steady you when you feel exposed. Day five hundred sixty-five.
